title: Redwood structured output + function calling demo - Trilogy Retail
summary: Redwood AE+SE demo of structured JSON output and function-calling workflow for Trilogy Retail. Covered JSON schemas, validation and guardrails, Console config for schema enforcement, and an end-to-end demo calling a mock inventory API from the model. Customer asked about latency/cost tradeoffs, dedicated vs hosted, and security controls (KMS and audit logs). Agreed next steps: send pricing + quantization guidance, share benchmark script and sample payloads, schedule a 1-hour POC kickoff next week.

transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-02-28 | Start: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 46m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Jenna Lee (Trilogy), Marco Ruiz (Trilogy), Samir Khan (Trilogy)

00:00 Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we really appreciate you carving out time. I'm Maya, I'm the AE on the account, and with me is Ravi our solutions engineer.
00:08 Ravi: Hi all, real quick agenda — we'll do a 20 minute demo of structured JSON output + function calling, then 15 for questions, and wrap with next steps. Cool?
00:16 Jenna: Sounds good. We're especially interested in making sure outputs are valid JSON and that we can safely call internal tools.
00:22 Marco: Yup and latency matters, we have a realtime replenishment flow so sub-200ms token latency is ideal, but we can trade if needed.
00:30 Maya: Great, good context. **Quick note** — some of the product names in the demo may be pronounced weirdly in the transcript, hope that's fine.

02:05 Ravi: Alright sharing my screen, first thing — JSON mode. This is the API param that pins the model to emit a structured JSON object. You can attach a schema (we support JSON Schema like patterns) and Redwood will validate and, if enabled, apply an auto-correction fallback or reject.
02:32 Marco: When you say "auto-correction fallback", does that mean you'd try to fix malformed JSON or call a function to re-request?
02:40 Ravi: Good question. We have two approaches: strict mode returns an error so your app can handle it, permissive mode tries to coerce into the schema using best-effort heuristics and we annotate the correction in the response metadata. Both have tradeoffs.
02:58 Maya: And in Console you can toggle the guardrail behavior per-route — e.g., for financial flows you probably want strict, for chat UI you might want permissive.

05:10 Speaker 1: (mumble) — there's also the function calling piece.
05:15 Ravi: Yes, function calling — the structured output can map directly to a function signature. In the demo I'm going to call a mock Inventory API function that updates stock. We'll show the JSON payload being validated against the schema and then the function invocation.
05:30 Marco: Is the function executed in Redwood infra, or do we run it in our environment?
05:36 Ravi: You have options: Redwood-hosted webhooks for convenience, or you can route calls to your private endpoint inside a VPC. For private deployments we support connector proxies and mTLS so calls never leave your network if you want.

07:45 Jenna: Security question — how does KMS fit here? If the model produces PII or we log function arguments, who has access?
07:55 Maya: We integrate with customer KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, HSM) for keys at rest. Audit logs are available in the Console and you can set log retention. For Private deployments you retain all logs on-prem. We are SOC 2 compliant and can share the report.

10:02 Ravi: Demo start — sample prompt: 'Return an update object for product sku 12345 with fields: sku, delta_qty, reason, timestamp'. I'm sending request in JSON mode and attaching schema.
10:20 (typing sounds)
10:40 Response arrives (structured): {
  "sku": "12345",
  "delta_qty": 10,
  "reason": "restock - unexpected sales spike",
  "timestamp": "2027-02-28T15:10:42Z"
}
10:55 Ravi: You can see it matched schema exactly, Redwood also returns a 'schema_match' boolean in the metadata.
11:12 Marco: Nice. If it didn't match, could we see the raw model output for auditing?
11:18 Ravi: Yes, raw_text is available in the response payload unless you disable raw logging. We also surface diffs in the Console.

13:30 Maya: Now function call flow — the model returns the same JSON but with a 'call_instruction' object we use to trigger the inventory update. I'm going to demo calling our mock function.
13:45 (Ravi clicks)
14:02 System: Function invocation logged -> webhook dispatched to https://mock-inventory.example.com/updateStock
14:10 (small lag)
14:18 System: 200 OK from webhook - inventory updated.
14:25 Jenna: Quick — what's the retry logic if webhook times out?
14:30 Ravi: Exponential backoff with configurable retries per-route. For mission-critical flows we recommend async function patterns — Redwood persists the call and retries until success or you hit max attempts.

16:05 Speaker 2: (crosstalk) can you talk about latency numbers for hosted vs dedicated?
16:12 Maya: Sure. Hosted API median token latency for these open models is around 50-80ms for short contexts. For strict latency SLOs we recommend Dedicated with pinned GPU pools — that gets you sub-30ms tail for common seq lengths, but cost goes up. We can run a benchmark with your payload shape.
16:35 Marco: What's the typical cost delta? ballpark?
16:38 Maya: Ballpark — Dedicated fixed commit plus lower per-token cost. We'll send a detailed comparison; depends on qps and sequence length and whether you enable continuous batching or KV caching.

19:00 Ravi: Now switching to Console — policy page. You can define route-level schema enforcement, function call enablement, and guardrail policies like max_tokens, max_string_length, allowed_domains for webhook targets, and role-based approvals for changes.
19:25 Samir: Approvals — is that integrated with SSO? We need SAML and SCIM to map roles.
19:32 Maya: Yes we support SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning and native RBAC. For audit we tie actions to user identities in the audit log.

22:10 Marco: One more technical — you mentioned KV cache earlier, is that safe across customers? We have multiple tenants.
22:18 Ravi: KV cache is per-deployment and per-model shard; for multi-tenant customers we use tenant-scoped caches. On Dedicated you can isolate caches to a pool. There was a minor slip earlier where someone said 'KV cash' in the docs, so watch for OCR-like errors in transcripts.

24:45 Jenna: If we implement strict JSON schema, how do we handle non-deterministic model outputs like synonyms or extra fields?
24:53 Ravi: A couple options — you can use a strict schema with patternProperties to allow synonyms, or use middleware in the function that normalizes fields. Redwood also supports a 'schema repair' feature that attempts minimal edits and records them. If you need total determinism, we'd recommend templated generation or a hybrid approach with reranking.

28:00 Maya: Quick peek at Redwood Optimize — it will suggest quantization and batching settings based on your workload. For example, for short inventory updates we might recommend int8 quant with per-token batching to lower cost by 40% while keeping 95th percentile latency within SLO.
28:25 Marco: Do you have real benchmarks on our hardware targets? We use A100s in one region and T4s elsewhere.
28:32 Ravi: We can run a benchmark on both. For A100 you'll see much better throughput for large batches; T4 is cost-efficient for bursty, small requests. We'll include a benchmark matrix.

31:10 Speaker 3: slight filler - so what about evals and QC?
31:18 Maya: You can run prompt sets as evals in Console, tie regression alerts to them, and get diffs when a model update changes structured output. We also store example-level traces for debugging.

33:50 Marco: Any caveats for function calling with private endpoints? e.g., latency from Redwood to our VPC?
33:56 Ravi: If you host the endpoint inside your VPC and use the Private deployment connector, calls stay within network fabric and latency is minimal. For hosted webhooks we recommend co-locating endpoints in same cloud region.

36:10 Jenna: Ok this is all helpful. What about error visibility — if function invocation fails mid-run, can we replay?
36:18 Ravi: Yes, we persist the request and provide a replay button in Console that replays the call with the same model output or re-evaluates the model. Replays are logged and can be gated with approvals.

39:05 Samir: One procurement/security question — will logs contain full payloads by default?
39:12 Maya: By default raw_text is captured but you can redact or disable raw logging per-route; we recommend token-level redaction for PII and integrating with your KMS for encrypted-at-rest logs.

41:40 Maya: Alright wrapping up — quick recap. We demoed JSON mode + schema enforcement, function calling with webhook and VPC options, Console guardrails, and Redwood Optimize suggestions.
41:55 Jenna: Next steps for us — we'll send peak qps and full schema, and we'd like the benchmark script.
42:03 Maya: Great. Action items noted — Ravi will upload the benchmark harness; I'll send pricing and onboarding links.

44:00 Marco: Thanks, that was useful. We'll get notes to decide between Hosted for quick rollout vs Dedicated POC.
44:08 Maya: Perfect. We'll follow up with calendar for the POC kickoff.
44:15 (meeting ends)
